It depends on when you define the cut-off date that distinguishes Germans and Austrians. The Habsburg dynasty claimed the title of the emperor of the Holy Roman Empire in the late medieval period and had yet its seat in Vienna in 1806 when Naüpoleon took it (and was by the Kaiserhymne known as "German emperor of German lands"), and it wasn't until 1871 that the Prussians forced a clear distinction between the new German Empire and Austria-Hungary.

I'd argue that that the Habsburg emperors' claim on Greater Germany was only nominal and without real consequence, so I would restrict Austrian contributions to those directly under Habsburg dominion. Which yet leaves us with a lot exploration of the Americas during the Age of Sail under Spanish Habsburg, great contributions to music under Beethoven and late Mozart. and Mises' Austrian circle contributing to macroeconomics.

Japan was highly insular until its forced opening in the late 19th century, and its advances in Buddhist teaching and in codifying the Hagakure were inconsequential outside its own culture. It only became an economic powerhouse post WW2, and no one will doubt what impact Japanese automotive engineering alone and the Lean Production it eschewed had in recent decades - and that is without the cultural impact Sega, Nintendo, Sony and anime had across the world.

In the end I would say that the contributions are too wildly disparate in their relevant time frame and their relative impact to allow for a direct comparison. What I can say is that we would have noticed if the contributions of either had been missing.
